headings.title: Introduction to Heartburn in Pregnancy
headings.content: Heartburn, medically known as **pyrosis**, is a burning sensation felt behind the breastbone caused by stomach acid flowing back up into the esophagus. It is one of the most common discomforts experienced during pregnancy, affecting up to eighty percent of expectant mothers, particularly as they approach the third trimester. While it rarely threatens the life of the mother or child, severe pyrosis significantly diminishes a pregnant woman's quality of life, disturbing sleep and daily nutrition. For student nurses, understanding this symptom is vital because pregnant women frequently seek safe, practical remedies during routine antenatal visits.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Pregnancy-Induced Acid Reflux
headings.content:
Two primary physiological forces drive heartburn in pregnant women: hormonal shifts and mechanical displacement. 

- **Progesterone**: This dominant pregnancy hormone relaxes smooth muscle tissue throughout the body, including the **lower esophageal sphincter (LES)**, allowing gastric acid to escape upward easily.
- **Gastric Motility**: High progesterone levels also slow down overall digestion, meaning food sits in the stomach longer and increases intra-gastric pressure.
- **Mechanical Pressure**: As the uterus enlarges, it physically displaces the stomach upward and crowds the abdominal cavity, shortening transit time and encouraging reflux.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Subjective Assessment
headings.content: When a pregnant patient complains of heartburn, nurses must listen carefully to the specific description of her discomfort. Typical signs include a burning sensation rising from the epigastric region toward the throat, a sour or bitter taste in the mouth, and occasional regurgitation of food particles or liquid. Symptoms frequently worsen after eating large meals, bending over, or lying flat on the back. Nurses should ask targeted assessment questions regarding the frequency, timing, and severity of these episodes to gauge how much the symptoms interfere with normal nutrition and rest.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Differential Diagnosis
headings.content: Not every chest discomfort in pregnancy is simple heartburn. Nurses must perform thorough assessments to rule out more serious cardiovascular or gastrointestinal conditions. A sharp, crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw or left arm, accompanied by shortness of breath or dizziness, requires immediate medical evaluation to rule out cardiac issues. Similarly, severe upper right quadrant pain might indicate gallbladder disease rather than normal pregnancy reflux. Careful history-taking helps differentiate benign pyrosis from pathology requiring urgent intervention.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological Management and Lifestyle Modifications
headings.content:
First-line management for pregnancy heartburn focuses entirely on lifestyle and dietary adjustments to minimize acid exposure. Nurses should educate patients using practical, everyday strategies:

- **Meal Frequency**: Eat small, frequent meals throughout the day instead of three large meals to prevent stomach over distension.
- **Postural Habits**: Remain upright for at least one to two hours after eating and avoid lying down immediately.
- **Sleep Elevation**: Elevate the head of the bed by six to nine inches using blocks to use gravity in keeping stomach acid down.
- **Dietary Triggers**: Avoid known triggers such as fatty foods, caffeine, chocolate, citrus fruits, and spicy dishes.

headings.title: Pharmacological Interventions and Safe Medications
headings.content: When lifestyle changes fail to control symptoms, safe pharmacological options may be introduced under medical supervision. Antacids containing calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide are typically the first choice because they neutralize existing stomach acid quickly. However, nurses must teach patients to avoid sodium bicarbonate, which can cause fluid retention and metabolic imbalances, and magnesium trisilicate in high doses. If antacids are insufficient, H2-receptor antagonists like famotidine may be prescribed. Proton pump inhibitors are generally reserved for severe, refractory cases after careful risk-benefit analysis by the primary healthcare provider.

headings.title: Patient Education and Potential Complications
headings.content: Persistent, untreated acid reflux can lead to complications such as esophagitis, mucosal erosion, or chronic sleep deprivation. Comprehensive patient education empowers the mother to manage symptoms safely while knowing when to seek professional help. Nurses should instruct patients to consult their midwife or doctor before purchasing any over-the-counter herbal remedies or new antacids, as some ingredients may be unsafe during pregnancy. Emphasizing compliance with dietary adjustments ensures a more comfortable pregnancy journey for both mother and child.
